lines.text: Right now, a machine built in 1977 is still sending us messages from more than twenty-four billion kilometres away.
And on Mars, another machine has said nothing at all for eight years.
Same agency. Same promise. Two very different endings.
I'm Md Mahiyan Noor Mahi, and this is Team Cosmic Eclipse from Sylhet, Bangladesh.
lines.say: I'm Mohammad Mahiyan Noor Mahi, and this is Team Cosmic Eclipse, from Sylhet, Bangladesh.

lines.text: My teammates are Maliha, team leader; Nuhza, designer; Fatema, data scientist; Omi, developer; Montaha, researcher; and finally, me, Mahi, the storyteller.
We kept asking one question: when a mission goes quiet, where does its story go?
Our answer is a website called Abandoned, But Not Forgotten.
Since the 1960s, NASA has left hardware on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space.
The facts exist. But they're scattered across mission pages, press releases, and PDFs.
And one word hides the truth: "abandoned."
Nobody drove these machines home. They worked until something stopped them.
Dust.
Cold.
Fading power.
Distance.
Opportunity was built to last ninety Martian days. It worked for more than fourteen years.
Then, in 2018, a global dust storm blocked its sunlight.
Engineers sent more than a thousand recovery commands. Nothing came back.
That's the part that matters most: why a mission ended. And it's the part hardest to find.
A student shouldn't need ten tabs to understand it.
So we built one place for it. Fifteen missions, from 1966 to today, across the Moon, Mars and deep space.
Scroll the homepage, and the story unfolds scene by scene, from leaving Earth to the final silence.
Follow six decades on the timeline, or find every machine on the hardware map.
Our Final Signal page separates four moments most people mix up: launch, arrival, last contact, and official closure.
Because "lost" and "finished" are not the same thing.
Pick a spacecraft and turn it around in 3D.
Or play Mission Detective. Read the clues about Spirit, Opportunity, or Surveyor 3, and work out what happened.
There's a quiz, a mission comparison, and a 3D game too.
Every fact comes from NASA and JPL sources.
And when a machine "speaks" in first person, we label it clearly as creative interpretation, never as a real transmission.
Why does this matter?
For a student, it turns space history from a list of dates into a set of stories with an ending, and a reason.
It's built with plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework, no backend, and most of it works offline.
So a classroom with a weak connection can still open it. That matters where we live.
And it's honest. Sources are on the site, and the line between fact and imagination is never blurred.
This is a first version, with fifteen missions. To take it further, we need three things:
experts to review and expand the archive,
access to more NASA imagery and 3D surface data,
and a Bangla version, with teacher resources, so schools here can use it.
Voyager is still talking. Opportunity went quiet.
Our job is to make sure both are heard.
Abandoned, But Not Forgotten.
